title: Gravity
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Gravity Worksheets (Mass, Weight and Newtons)
standard_text: Explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity acting between the Earth and the falling object.
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on gravity: why objects fall, mass and weight, newtons, weight on the Moon and other planets, and Newton and Galileo. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Weight is the pull of gravity, in newtons; mass stays the same everywhere.
body_html:
How to think about it

Gravity pulls unsupported objects towards the centre of the Earth.

  • Mass is the amount of matter (kg). Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, a force measured in newtons (N).
  • On Earth, each kilogram weighs about 10 N. On the Moon, gravity is about one-sixth as strong, so weight is less but mass is the same.
  • Without air, all objects fall at the same rate (Galileo, Newton).
Example

Mass 4 kg on Earth. Weight?

4 × 10

Answer: 40 N

Example

Weighs 600 N on Earth. On the Moon?

600 ÷ 6

Answer: 100 N

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up mass and weight.
  • Writing weight in kilograms.
  • Thinking heavier objects always fall faster.

faq.a: A force of attraction between objects. The Earth's gravity pulls unsupported objects towards its centre, which is why things fall.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms. Weight is the force of gravity on it, in newtons. On Earth, 1 kg weighs about 10 N.

faq.q: Would I weigh less on the Moon?
faq.a: Yes. The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so your weight would be about one-sixth. Your mass would stay the same.
